slides.narration: Welcome to Book III, Chapter 20: Designing Algorithms for Real Hardware. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. In algorithms, beauty is not enough. Every procedure needs a specification, a correctness argument, a cost model, and a witness that lets us inspect behavior.

Learners should be able to explain why the algorithm is correct, what input size or structure controls cost, and what output or trace proves the implementation followed the intended procedure. question.prompt: Why is passing one test not the same as proving an algorithm?
question.answer: A test samples behavior. A proof or invariant explains why the procedure works for the stated input domain; tests then serve as witnesses and regression guards.

slides.title: 20.1.2 Improving Temporal Locality
keyPoints: Temporal locality means recently used data is accessed again before it is displaced.
Blocking a matrix computation into tiles can improve reuse when several operations consume the same region.
A tile that is too large can defeat the purpose, while a tiny tile can add unnecessary loop overhead.
Choose dimensions through workload-aware measurement.
slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 20, treat 20.1.2 Improving Temporal Locality as an algorithmic claim. Temporal locality means recently used data is accessed again before it is displaced. Blocking a matrix computation into tiles can improve reuse when several operations consume the same region. A tile that is too large can defeat the purpose, while a tiny tile can add unnecessary loop overhead. Choose dimensions through workload-aware measurement. For records {x,y,z}, an array of structures keeps each record’s fields together. That can suit operations that consume all fields of one record. Separate x, y, and z arrays can suit operations scanning one field across many records, reducing irrelevant field traffic and potentially simplifying vectorization. A time difference may reflect cache misses, instruction count, vectorization, page translation, frequency changes, or interference. Timing alone does not identify the cause. slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 20, treat Failure clinic — A faster benchmark computes less work as an algorithmic claim. A developer moves result consumption out of a benchmark and stops checking the sum. The compiler can now prove that the computed value is unused and remove work. The apparent speedup measures the absence of the required computation. Restoring observable output is necessary, but the broader lesson is that benchmark code is still ordinary optimized C++ and must obey the same semantic reasoning as application code. Another experiment initializes one candidate’s data before timing but includes initialization for the other. The resulting comparison mixes layout cost with traversal cost asymmetrically. Either include preparation for both under an end-to-end contract or exclude it for both under a kernel-only contract. Both experiments can be useful; only the undisclosed mismatch is misleading.
